subtopic: MR. THOMPSON-LETTER TO MR. SPEAKER ON PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE
MR. THOMPSON-LETTER TO MR. SPEAKER ON PARLIAMENTARY PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of personal privilege regarding a letter which I wrote to Your Honour on October 4, 1963, following my return from New Zealand and Australia, outlining some of my observations on the manner in which the parliaments in Canberra and Wellington carry on their procedures. I have not made any statement to the public or to the press, nor have I written any subsequent letter to Your Honour about this subject as reported in a press release across the nation on Saturday.
Knowing of your great interest and concern in the reform of parliamentary procedure, I wrote to you giving my impressions of what I had observed in Australia and New Zealand. In this regard I must commend Your Honour for the reports of your special committee and the commendable work which has been done, the results of which have been outlined in the various reports submitted to
this house. I regard the fifteenth report of the committee on procedure and organization, which is now before this house, as the most important and wide reaching of all. I trust that it will be favourably received and adopted this session.
I first heard of the Saturday news report when a reporter from my home town paper, the Red Deer Advocate, telephoned me yesterday asking for verification and enlargement of this press statement. The statement, as he read it to me, indicated that I had suggested elimination of the $6,000 tax free expense allowance now paid to members of parliament, believing that in so doing a great deal would be accomplished toward restoring parliament's public image.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I must categorically deny that I ever recommended the elimination of a member of parliament's expense allowance. I know all too well personally that this allowance is not more than adequate to cover the expenses of a member of this house who conscientiously endeavours to fulfil his responsibilities to his constituents and to the nation, particularly in the case of those who represent distant constituencies.
My purpose in writing to you, now more than 17 months ago, was with the thought that my observations would be of benefit to the special committee on procedure and organization which you planned to establish. On March 16, 1964 you replied, stating your own interest in my comments about Australia and New Zealand and informing me that you were referring a summary of my comments to the committee for their consideration.
Since that date I have not made any statements to the public or to the press, with the exception of last Thursday morning when Mr. Richard Jackson of the Ottawa Journal questioned me on how my comments to you regarding the Australian procedure would affect the Canadian situation. His comments were part of his "Hill Talk'' column in Saturday's Ottawa Journal, and were basically correct. According to this, in lieu of the $6,000 now allowed each member of parliament a system such as that used in Australia would provide for a member of parliament's expenses in a more equitable and direct manner. How the national news report came to be

Questions
circulated across the nation I do not know, except that I am given to understand it was a mistake that it was worded in the way it was and entirely misrepresented the remarks I had made in my original letter.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me this point of privilege to clarify a situation which has given a completely false interpretation of my original remarks.

speechtext: Have the qualifications and standards of training of penitentiary staff changed since 1963 and, if so, in what respects?

subtopic: CHANGES IN PENITENTIARY STAFF TRAINING
speechtext:
Since January 1, 1963, the following changes in the penitentiary staff training programs have taken place, resulting in an over-all higher standard of knowledge and physical ability:
(a)	Policy directives and instructions have been issued to each institution on the type of training to be undertaken within each institution. This includes, in addition to review training, the conduct of basic instruction training and basic relations training courses.
(b)	A continuous training program is in effect at the three correctional staff colleges.
Questions
This program includes induction training courses (three months) for all custodial recruits; methods of instruction courses; basic administration courses; correctional officer courses; instructor workshops for all staff training officers; senior officer courses.

(d)	Prerequisites for potential course candidates are set for each specific course and include, amongst other things, position level concerned, satisfactory completion of specific institutional and/or penitentiary courses, as well as the appropriate level of physical ability.

REPORT ON FLUORIDATION
speechtext:
1.	Have studies designed to confirm or refute Dr. Rapaport's unconvincing observations been undertaken in Canada and, if so, were they supported by the Department of National Health and Welfare?
2.	In the past, when unconvincing preliminary results have raised doubts as to the safety of a food additive, what procedures has the department followed for the protection of Canadian consumers?
3.	Are the same procedures being applied with regard to fluoride, which is undoubtedly being added to canned and other processed foods packed by plants using fluoridated city waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORT ON FLUORIDATION
speechtext:
1. The department is not aware of authentic evidence indicating that any ill effects have ever been encountered in North America by consumption of water fluoridated at one part per million. On the contrary, there are many reports in the scientific literature attesting to the safety and value of fluoridation as a public health measure. Studies designed to confirm or refute Dr. Rapaport's data relating to fluoridation in Wisconsin have not therefore been undertaken by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
2 and 3. Officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare are continually searching the literature for reports of adverse effects from the ingestion of any component of a food. Such reports are carefully scrutinized and weighed against the body of available scientific information. If there is sufficient evidence action is initiated to reduce or eliminate the hazards. These procedures are being applied to fluoride.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a non-controversial question to the Prime Minister. It arises in connection with the reference you made a moment ago to the pride of Canadians in the success of Miss Petra Burka and other champions in the field of sport.
Without in any way being critical of the showing of the Canadian team in the world hockey championships, and recognizing the great importance to national and international prestige of success being attained in fields of athletics-particularly the degree to which success in athletics has its influence among nations which believe in freedom and among communist nations-would the government give consideration to preparing now for future competitions in the field of hockey by utilizing the fitness and amateur sports council that was set up under the government of which I had the honour to be prime minister, and set up a committee of parliament-and there are many representatives of various sports who have had great success in the house-to the end that we will assure hereafter that Canada's representation in the field of international competition, particularly in amateur sport, shall be of the very best?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minisler):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SUGGESTED SETTING UP OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman's question is, as he said, entirely non-controversial, but our method of participation in world hockey championships is, I believe, less non-controversial; and I may say in the present circumstances I have no particular desire to enter into the controversy on how we should participate. But I do agree with my hon. friend that this is an important matter and that it could very well be considered along the lines he has indicated.
One of our difficulties, of course, especially in hockey, lies in finding amateur hockey players to participate in so-called amateur tournaments. So highly skilled is our participation in hockey generally that practically every good player in Canada under the age of ten is on the negotiating list, at least, of some professional club. This makes it difficult to secure and keep together a representative group of players. However, I will be glad to take this matter up with the minister concerned, whose interest in hockey is, I know, equal to my own.

subtopic: SUGGESTED SETTING UP OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext: A supplementary question to the Prime Minister following a question I asked some two weeks ago concerning amateur sport. speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SUGGESTED SETTING UP OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am afraid I have forgotten the question the hon. member asked earlier on this subject, but I can say to him now that this government, like the previous government, does help amateur teams going abroad to take part in international competitions, though the amount of the assistance varies.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. About a week ago I asked whether the Canadian government had extended their peace keeping mandate in Cyprus. I believe the time has now passed when this expired. What is the position of the government in this regard?

The secretary general, I understand, has indicated that it is desirable in his judgment that the force continue to operate on the island; and that there should be no reduction in the numbers, as was rumoured, in spite of the financial situation facing the United Nations. speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: CHARNY, QUE.-STATEMENT ON DOOR TO DOOR DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) asked the Prime Minister a question about the interpretation of a reply I had given to one of his questions put on the order paper, which reply was tabled in the house on March 10, 1965. That question concerned the interpretation of the extension of a letter carrier service from a main locality. Here is the answer to that question asked by the hon. member for Megantic.
The basic requirement for the establishment of an independent letter carrier service is the presence of 2,500 delivery points in a concentrated and built-up area.
However, if two or more neighbouring localities have together the required number of delivery points, a letter carrier service may be established if those localities agree. Such an agreement is necessary because, under such circumstances, the post office of the most important locality becomes, normally, the dispatching point for mailmen and, at the same time, post offices in smaller localities are closed down and replaced by sub-offices of the new letter carrier post office.
When the density of homes in an area next to a locality with letter carrier service permits the establishment of such a service on

an economic basis, it may be established irrespective of the number of delivery points.
That does not constitute the establishment of a new independent letter carrier service, but simply the extension of a service already in existence.
The letter carrier service recently established in Charny is an extension of the Levis letter carrier service.
Besides Levis, letter carriers of the Levis post office are serving the St. David de l'Aube-Riviere, St. Telesphore and St. Romuald d'Et-chemin, localities in the immediate vicinity, on the western side of Levis. The 1,080 delivery points in Charny, a locality adjacent to St. Romuald d'Etchemin, get a home delivery service which is merely an extension of the service already given in the surrounding area.
In short, in order to set up an independent letter carrier service there must be 2,500 delivery points, but where such a service is already existing it can be extended to other delivery points no matter what the number is; there is no minimum.

That Bill C-136, now before the house, be amended to authorize, in the place of the age adjusted pension now provided for by part IV of the said bill, that a pension under the Old Age Security Act in the full amount of the pension available to those who have attained 70 years of age be paid commencing 1 January 1966 to those who have attained 69 years of age, commencing 1 January 1967 to those who have attained 68 years of age, commencing 1 January 1968 to those who have attained 67 years of age, commencing 1 January 1969, to those who have attained 66 years of age, and commencing 1 January 1970 to those who have attained 65 years of age.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sorry it was not possible for me to be here on Friday, but since then I have had the opportunity of reading Hansard and I wish to comment that I would have thought the Minister of National Health and Welfare would have learned her lesson by this time. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I quite agree they are not, but I appreciate that a certain amount of leniency must have been shown to the minister on Friday.
Briefly, this resolution is preliminary to amending part IV of the bill by progressively reducing the age limit to 65 years, starting January 1, 1966, for the receipt of old age security of $75 a month. Under the government's previous proposal it would have been possible to receive an actuarially reduced old age pension, but now the full amount of $75 old age security will be paid; and we are in complete accord with this.
There is also an income tax amendment involved which will take away the automatic exemption of $500 extra per year granted those who have reached 65, and keep it from them until they reach age 70. I had hoped this would not have been the case, but as we are anxious to see the amendment which the minister will propose we will agree to the resolution.

Canada Pension Plan

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Could the minister tell the committee what were the considerations which induced the government to give the full old age pension on an age reducing scale, something which was not proposed by the special joint committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hon. members will recall that the principle of paying pensions at 65 was part of the Canada pension plan from the beginning, but payments were to be scaled down from the full amount at age 70. Two considerations were involved. One was the increase in revenue arising from taxation, as indicated by the Minister of National Revenue on Friday last, and the second stemmed from a recommendation of the special joint committee with respect to people who at the moment and in the future could not be contributors to the Canada pension plan, people who are at or about the age of 65 years.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Then I assume some of the discussions which took place in the special joint committee were responsible for the change in government policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

If it is only a question of money-and I realize, of course, that is a very big question-I do not understand why we cannot do this. I do not know on what principle we say that under the law of Canada one person should be able to benefit by social legislation and another person should not be able to benefit.

I am quite sure the government will not take all the credit for that or for the training program for our young people. We are looking to the future and are willing to go into the red temporarily to pay for the education of our young people. Why not pay our old people, who have already earned their way, what is coming to them? Why should they not be allowed to share in this 37 per cent, 18 per cent and 54 per cent profit that we are showing? If it is only paper profit, let us share the paper profit with them, and do it now. Why wait five years?
Many of us are at my advanced age. My father and mother may not live another five years. So if we are going to have this social
Canada Pension Plan
legislation well on into the future, it will liot benefit my father and mother nor the parents of many other people. If it is only a matter of money, come out straight and let us say so and let us pass it and have a deficit budget. When this party was running the nation's affairs we budgeted for a deficit for the needs of the Canadian people, and it has paid off magnificently. We invested in our future, and you people over there are riding the crest of this wave. We used our imagination and this vision which you laughed at so much, and it paid off. We built railways into the north country, and they are bringing ore out already.
Our old people who pioneered that country and went in there when there were no railroads and no security of this kind whatsoever should receive this benefit now. If we are so prosperous, why put it off until tomorrow? Do it now. Why wait till spring? Why wait' till the spring of 1970? Let us do it now. Believe me, if you bring in an amendment yourselves, or will listen to an amendment of ours and pass it, you will find an unanimity in this house that you have not seen for years.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: This is getting to be socialism.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

No, I am not getting to be a socialist. I am willing to share with the old people for what they did for me. My education was paid for by my father and mother, and now that I am able to make a decent living I am willing to share it with them. If it means an increase in taxes, let us be honest and pay it now. Let us take it out of this year's or next year's revenue. If we are not prosperous, tell us the truth. If Canada cannot afford to pay it in an election year, tell us the truth; tell us we are broke. But you know we are not; this country was never so well off.
I think we have all shared in this. I do not pretend it was only this party that was responsible for it. Peril a p s other people over there also worked for it. The old people worked for it, and I think it is time we paid them off. And don't throw socialism at me; there is a great deal of difference between social security and socialism, as everybody knows.
We owe this money, as a matter of fact. It is just a question of paying our debts. We are not afraid to go into debt in time of war, for national security; and we should not be afraid to go into debt in time of peace to pay off our old people. I am consistent about this. I spoke two weeks ago in the house and suggested we should pay them $100 a month and not $75; and I think we can pay

that. Probably 25 years from now, when we look back at these days of prosperity, we will wonder why we did not pay it. To me this bill appears to be a dream of bureaucracy.

Perhaps this could

then be extended to cover those individuals who will not be covered under the present provisions. As I look through this resolution I find that in one year certain individuals will receive benefits and in other years certain other individuals will receive the same benefits, on a progressing basis; but I should like to impress upon the ministers concerned that this procedure could also take place in reverse. While I realize that in any legislation of this kind a line must be drawn, when this line is drawn people who find themselves on the wrong side will be disappointed. If we are going to phase out old age security provisions and save a certain amount of money by doing so, let us do so at this time, and use the savings to enlarge the benefits payable under the Canada pension plan.
I do not intend to compare old age security with the pension plan, but I would suggest that the resolution now before us for consideration represents the greatest possible criticism of the pension plan. I will confine my remarks at this point to clause 119, as required by the rules. I have circulated all the amendments at once but I do so purely as a matter of convenience for all hon. members so they can see the proposed amendments together.
With regard to clause 119, subsection (1) of section 3 of the Old Age Security Act will
Canada Pension Plan
now provide for the payment of a pension of the full amount to persons who attain the age of 65. However, this must be read in conjunction with clause 122, which sets out the progressive stages by which the pension at the reduced age becomes available, commencing in January, 1966 in respect to persons who have attained the age of 69 years, and so on, down to age 65 in 1970.
Section 3 (1) (b) (ii), as contained in clause 119, implements recommendation No. 8 (b) (i) of the report of the special committee. This adds a third ground of eligibility based on residence and should overcome all possible objections in respect to persons who have spent the greater part of their working lives in Canada and who are not able to meet the present residence requirements. It will prove helpful to many persons who, for one reason or another, leave Canada before the age of 65 but who have spent virtually all of their working period in Canada. It will enable such persons to make application on attaining the age of 65, subject of course to the provisions of clause 122, and be granted a pension without having to return to Canada to re-establish residence, as is the case at present. It will be particularly helpful in the case of younger wives of pensioners who have left Canada with their husbands and established residence elsewhere. Pensions are payable out of Canada to persons otherwise eligible who have resided in Canada for 25 years since age 21. The 40 year period will therefore automatically cover this requirement. This will meet a problem which my predecessor, I am sure, will remember gave rise on occasion to difficult cases, about which I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has at various times made representations to the government.

speechtext:
Perhaps I was trying to alert the members on this side of the house to be here as well.
The other point of substance that is effected by the revised clause 119 is, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare pointed out, the implementation of recommendation No. 8 (4) of the committee, in which the committee urged that something be done about the position in which many people find themselves who have had to leave the country and are not able to come back for the one last year in order to qualify for their pension under the Old Age Security Act.
We have been over this a good many times in the House of Commons and we went over it pretty thoroughly in the committee. I have a good many letters in my files from various ministers of national health and welfare saying that this change could not be made. Now it is going to be made, and in my experience, which I am sure must be the experience of others, it is going to mean a great deal to a good many people who have had to go to some other clime for reasons of health or had to return to the United Kingdom or some such part of the world. As a matter of fact, I have taken the trouble to check all of the cases which I currently have in my files and this provision for 40 years, which some people when they first see it regard as quite lengthy, does cover every case; and I suspect that my experience in this regard is similar to that of others. These are people who have lived here until 65 or 68, or perhaps the husband has reached 70 and the wife has not, and because it is difficult to come back these people cannot get a pension. Now they will be able to do so. We are doing something for people who

have, in my view, earned this right. However they have left the country. They cannot vote for or against anybody in Canada. We are doing something for people that ought to be done for them. I am glad that this recommendation of the special joint committee has been accepted by the government and that it is here as part of clause 119 in its amended form.

I should like to say a word or two on this clause 119. It does, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, have two main points. It brings the age at which one might be a recipient of old age security down to 65. I think this next matter has been looked after as well as can be expected. There is a problem which the minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have both mentioned, that is the provision in the act to the effect that an applicant has to be in Canada for the last year prior to making his or her application for old age security. This rule has caused a real hardship amongst people. It has now been suggested that as long as an applicant has been in Canada for 40 years following his or her eighteenth birthday, that person should receive the pension. Some may complain about this length of time, because it brings a person to 58 years of age. I should like to think this is really the prime of life and one may have many useful years ahead.
I really have not had the time to consider this 40 year period. It may meet the need, but I am just wondering if by any chance there is the possibility it goes too far. However, we certainly wish to support clause 119, I am pleased to see this change has been made from the provisions of the old part IV of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I move:
The said act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 3 thereof, the following section:
"3A. (1) The basic amount of the monthly pension that may be paid to any person is $75.
(2)	Where, either before or after the coming into force of this section, a pension has been authorized to be paid to any person, the amount of such pension shall be adjusted annually, in such manner as may be prescribed by regulation, so that the amount that may be paid to such person for a month in any year after 1967 is the product obtained by multiplying
(a) the basic amount of such pension, by
Canada Pension Plan
(b) the ratio that the pension index for that year bears to the pension index for the year 1967.
(3)	In this section, "pension index" has the meaning assigned by section 20 of the Canada pension plan, and the pension index for any year means the pension index for that year calculated as provided in that section.
Section 121, part IV of Bill C-136 added three new sections, as sections 3A, 3B and 3C respectively. Section 120 as amended, merely adds one section as section 3A which is adapted from 3C as set out in section 121 of part IV. This provided for an annual adjustment of pension in line with the rises in the pension index which is referred to in clause 20 of the bill. This will permit adjustments to be made after December, 1967 in accordance with rises in the cost of living.
The new section makes one small addition to the former section 3C in specifically defining the basic amount of the monthly pension as $75.

I should like to say a few words in regard to clause 120, more specifically with regard to the pension index. This clause provides that, in the future, the old age pension will be automatically adjusted by way of the pension index. The pension index is really just a consumer price index. One of the explanations given by the government for the inclusion of this automatic escalation of old age security is to remove it from the sphere of political pressure. In other words the pension will be automatically increased as the consumer price index goes up.
My contention is that if the old age security pension is to be increased, the pension index is not the proper yardstick. I would prefer to see the old age security treated in a prescribed manner, say by way of an advisory committee that would periodically decide or recommend to the government how much they considered the old age security pension should be properly increased. My contention is that, in view of the fact the pension index is not a proper index for adjusting old age security, there will be pressures in the future on the government to change the index used.
In support of my contention that the pension index is not the proper index to use, I made a few rough calculations with regard to the effect of the consumer price index in the future on the amount of the old age security pension, and the effect on old age security if other indices were applied. I contend that if the pension is realistic now at $75 per month, then in order to retain that same relationship between the $75 per month and the average earnings of Canadians today,

Canada Pension Plan
the index that should be used is not only the index for the gross national product but also the average earnings of all Canadians.
The proposal here is that if the consumer price index goes up by less than 1 per cent, then there is no adjustment in the old age security pension in the following year. These small increases of less than 1 per cent gradually accumulate, and when they accumulate to 1 per cent there is an adjustment. Moreover, if the consumer price index goes up by more than 2 per cent, then the maximum adjustment is only 2 per cent. As an example, the maximum increase could take place in the old age security pension by 1968, and that would be the first year of the adjustment. It would amount to $1.50 per month, which is a bit less than a quarter of the six bucks about which everybody has heard.
If you take the experience of the period 1946 to 1963, that is about a 17 year period, you find that the gross national product index per capita in terms of current dollars would have increased something over 100 per cent. Now, the experience of the consumer price index would have indicated an increase of only 73 per cent. Again, if you take the average weekly wage between 1946 and 1953, the increase is about 159 per cent. Therefore assuming-and one can logically assume- that the experience of the past will be somewhat duplicated in the future, it is obvious that the old age security pension will lag in relation to average earnings. Surely the real test of whether or not a retirement pension is adequate is the relationship of that pension to the average earnings and spending of Canadians. This was amply demonstrated in evidence given to the special committee, particularly by Mr. W. M. Anderson.
Taking the same figures in the consumer price index, between 1946 and 1963 there was an increase of 73 per cent. If the old age security pension was to be adjusted by this increase, then during that period the $75 would be increased by about $40, but by virtue of the fact no consumer price increase of more than 2 per cent in any one year will be applied to the old age pension, if you employ that feature of the government's proposal then, according to my rough calculations, during the 17 years I have listed the old age pension would go up by some $25, which is distinctly different from what the actual increase in the consumer price index would be.
In summary, if the government feels the old age security should be indexed, then the

index that should be employed should be such as to maintain the constant ratio between $75 and the present average earnings, so that that relationship would apply at all times. I hope the minister will give consideration to this. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has talked along these lines and I trust the minister will give it consideration so that the adjustments made in future to old age security pensions will be realistic.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have said a good many times during the course of consideration of the Canada pension plan that I regard as one of its most ingenious and useful arrangements the wage indexing scheme under which the rate of pensions is adjusted at the time they are put in pay. But I cannot understand that a government which was smart enough-maybe it was the civil servants who had the wisdom-to come up with such an ingenious and socially progressive principle, lets it die once people go on pension.
What we have done by working out this wage index and applying it, as we do, when putting pensions into pay, is to give people at the point at which they retire the full benefit-maybe the word "full" is too strong but I do not think it is-of the changes that have taken place in the economy while they have been working. Their pensions are calculated, not on the basis of the absolute dollars they earned, 10, 20, 30 or 40 years ago, but are calculated in the terms of the proportion their income has been of the accepted wage index. This is a means whereby people when they retire get pensions that are realistically related to the wage standards of that time, to the economy, to the affluence, the gross national product-to any of these indicators.
It seems to me that if we have been smart enough to come up with this kind of plan to put pensions into pay on a realistic basis, we should use that same principle from that point on. But no, we use the wage index up to the point of retirement and after people have retired the only indexing in the pensions they get is in accordance with the changes in the cost of living.
I can see it is an advance to get the principle of indexing of pensions that have been put in pay on the statute books. I have been asking for this for retired civil servants, C.N.R. employees and other groups all during the years I have been in this chamber. I think the idea that once pensions have been put in pay they should stay at a set figure until the recipients die is completely inhuman

and antisocial. It is good to get this principle started, but if we were smart enough to work out this wage index scheme for calculating pensions at the time they are put in pay, why not use the same ingenious arrangement, the same progressive approach, to the indexing of pensions after they have been put in pay?
We have all recognized that when people retire their pensions should bear a relationship to the economic conditions of that time. In other words, when a person retires at 65 his pension should relate to conditions when he is 65, not to conditions when he was 20. In my view the same consideration that brought us to this conclusion should apply to people after they retire.
After a person retires the cost of living, as statistics of the past indicate, continues to go up. Now the government says, "All right, we are going to help people cope with that rising cost of living." But other things change as well. The wage index goes up; other people are getting more wages. The affluence of the country goes up. The gross national product goes up. New things are brought on to the market.
There was a day when people retired and there were no television sets. In my view, when television came into being people who had retired before then had just as much right to income to buy television sets as people working at that time. We have no idea of the changes that will take place in our economy, in our standard of living, in our affluence, if you will, in the years after people retire. I suggest these changes that take place in the climate around our people, even if they are improvements in our standards of living, even if there is greater affluence, are just as much factors in the lives of retired people as they are in the lives of working people.
Since we are accepting the principle that as conditions improve people should share in those conditions, we should give our retired people the benefit of the best index we have been able to work out. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has given some statistics. No doubt he culled them from the same table I have in front of me, and though I suspect I may have done so before I would like to put some of these figures on the record.

speechtext:
In fact some of the promises of 1919 have not been acted on yet. This table is to be found at page 151 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special joint committee, in the issue for Wednesday December 2, 1964. There are four columns in the table. One is the gross national product at market prices in current dollars; the second is the gross national product at market prices on a per capita basis; the third is the consumer price index with 1949 being regarded as 100; and the fourth contains average weekly salaries and wages. Some of these columns start in 1926. The first year in which there is a figure in all four columns in 1939. So I should like to give the figures for 1939 and 1963 in all four of these columns.
The gross national product at market prices in current dollars in the aggregate was $5,636,000 in 1939. It was $43,007,000 in 1963 which is an increase of seven times or more. On a per capita basis it was $500. This is the gross national product at current prices. It was $500 in 1939; $2,276 in 1963-it had more than quadrupled. This is the gross national product on a per capita basis. I am now going over to the fourth column. Average weekly salaries and wages in 1939 were $23.44. In 1963 the figure is $83.41, again a multiplication of nearly four times. The last two quantities I have given are the significant ones. The gross national product on a per capita basis has gone up by more than four times between 1939 and 1963. Average weekly salaries and wages increased by almost four times. But we notice in the third column that the consumer price index in 1939 was 63.2 while in 1963 it was 133. That is an increase of only slightly more than twice.
So here, if I may eliminate the first of the four columns for the purpose of comparison, we have three scales. We have an increase in the gross national product on a per capita basis amounting to almost four times. We have weekly salaries and wages going up almost four times. But we pick out for our older people the consumer price index which has only gone up twice; we give them the benefit of the slowest moving index of the three.

Canada Pension Plan
What I am concerned about is not just that we have picked out something which is mathematically to the disadvantage of our older people. I am concerned about the fact that we do not seem willing to recognize- certainly this clause does not recognize it- that our older people are entitled not only to have their pensions protected against increases in the cost of living, but that they are also entitled to have their pension income protected so as to meet increases in the standard of living. Remember, they are still Canadian citizens; they are still part of the Canadian family. The changes which take place in the standard of living and in the climate about us are just as real to them as they are to working people or to the younger people. People who are still working will be seeking and getting increases in salaries and wages when they have an opportunity to do so. Those opportunities, in our experience, are implemented. But there are also these other people, and they will number millions as the years go by, to whom we shall say: No, the only adjustment we will give you in your pensions is in respect to the cost of living index; you will still be able to buy the same basket of goods and services as you did when this legislation was first introduced, but do not expect anything else in the basket; do not expect to share in improvements in our economy or in the growing affluence of our society.
In my view this is far from good enough. I acknowledge the minister's statement the other day that the $75 figure contained in this clause is not fixed for all time. That is an admission of something I have always known to be a fact-you do not take the pension question out of politics by any kind of legislation. And I am not sure there is anything wrong in that. After all, what is politics but the right to concern ourselves with things which concern our people? And one of the things which concern the people of this country is their standard of living. So I see nothing wrong with the whole question of pensions continuing to be a political issue. To say to our older people that the kind of adjustment they can expect is of the order of 75 cents or $1.50 at the most on a $75 basis, while others are getting much more substantial increases and when our gross national product is rising, seems to me to be entirely unsatisfactory.
Despite all the representations which have been made, clause 120 is the same as it was when the bill was brought in; it has remained unchanged throughout all the discussions which took place in the committee. I think

the government should tell us why they are not prepared to take the good and ingenious wage index scheme they used to put pensions in pay on a proper basis, and relate it to pensions after they have been put into pay as well. I agree we should have an index, but we should use the index which is best and most favourable to our older people. The cost of living index is not good enough. The wage index is the one which should be used in this clause.

I think all of us have been concerned by the fact that pensions lose their buying power over the years. People who are obliged to live on pensions or fixed incomes have suffered because of increases in the cost of living. I think it is most desirable there should be stability in the purchasing power of dollars derived from pensions or fixed incomes.
But I am not at all sure we should be trying to secure this result through the method set out in the bill before us, that is, by relating pensions to the price index. I believe some appropriate body might be set up to adjust pensions periodically as needed in accordance with the consumer price index, but I do not believe pensions should be tied automatically to the price index. It seems to me we are setting a dangerous precedent here.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre told us he had been advocating an extension of this system into many different fields. I believe we could easily reach a stage, if we pursued this line far enough, at which we would lose all responsibility and restraint in connection with maintaining the purchasing power of the dollar at an even level. We might reach the position where this type of indexing would extend so as to cover bonds, annuities and a whole field of activity. The labour unions might say, if this principle were established, that wages should be tied automatically to the consumer price index. I think this is a most dangerous precedent and I ask you, Mr. Chairman, where it will stop once we get started on this process. I think we should at this time be prepared to give serious consideration to the future in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I really do not think I can add anything to what I said in connection with clause 20 of the Canada pension plan proper. Exactly the same argument as was put forward by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was put forward on that particular clause. The government of Canada, in first attaching an index to pensions in pay is indeed taking a unique step in Canadian pensions. I believe this is the only pension plan in the 97-year history of this country that has been attached to an index. It was decided that once a person comes into pension-that is, once they have a pension in pay-the purchasing power of this pension should be sustained at the level it was when it went into pay; and thus the pension index has been established so that all pensions in pay will be adjusted by the changes in the cost of living index.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has pointed to the wages index which is used as an earnings index to adjust the amount of the average of his earnings on which a contribution is made over the years to calculate the pension which a person gets on retirement, and he has put forward the argument that this earnings index is the index that should also be used to adjust pensions in pay. Of course, in putting his argument forward he looks back at the period of the past 20 years when earnings increased at rates greatly in excess of increases in the cost of living and, he says this will give a higher amount to the pensions in pay. Certainly it would. But it would also be much more costly to the exchequer. Just as in the Canada pension plan, it was decided that the most the government could reasonably do in adjusting pensions in pay was to use the pension index, which is based on the cost of living index, as a means of guaranteeing that once a person is pensioned he will at least retain the purchasing power of the amount of the pension he got when he first was retired.
I really do not think I can say any more in addition to what I said when explaining the pension index and the earnings index back on clause 20.

Mr. Chairman, last Friday I believe the minister said that the present 3-3-4 tax would support the increases now proposed, including the increase by way of the consumer price index. Can the minister
Canada Pension Plan
say whether he has had any figures prepared as to what would be the situation with the old age security fund if the earnings index were used rather than the consumer price index?

Mr. Chairman, I am
astounded by the admission just made by the minister. Two weeks ago we asked for an economic report on the old age security fund, and we have not received it. nomic report on old age security would mean anything.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

Mr. Chairman, there is one other aspect of this clause about which I think something should be said, and one or two of my colleagues might have something to say in this connection as well. This is the clause that determines that the amount of the old age security pension is to remain at $75 a month. We are dealing with an amendment to clause 120, subclause 3A(1), thereof, which reads as follows:
The basic amount of the monthly pension that may be paid to any person is $75.
Everyone knows that there are many people in this country who feel that the time has come to increase the amount of this pension, and we feel-for reasons that I have given a good many times and therefore do not need to repeat-that it should be raised to $100 a month. We feel very strongly that the pleasure with which the Canada pension plan will be welcomed in this country once it is implemented, despite what some newspaper editorial writers are saying, is going to be dimmed by the fact that there has not been provided at the same time an increase in the pension of those who are now on old age security. Everyone knows that if it were possible under the rules of the house for a private member to move that the figure of $75 be changed to $100, that is precisely what I would be moving at this point. But everyone knows, also, that there is not any trick of the rules by which a private member could move such a motion at this stage of our proceedings. I have drafted the appropriate motion, Mr. Chairman; the only trouble is that I cannot put my name at the top of it. I will read the motion and then I will send it across.
The motion reads:
Moved by the Minister of-
-blank:
"That the amendment to clause 120 be amended by deleting the words seventy five dollars from subclause 3A (1) thereof, and by substituting therefor the words 'one hundred dollars' ".

I would like the messenger to take this over to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and she can decide which minister ought to move it. Perhaps she feels because she moved the original motion she should not move this one. The Minister of National Revenue has already moved an amendment so he cannot move this one, but I see the Secretary of State for External Affairs sitting, in his seat. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

Mr. Chairman, I can assure my hon. friend that nothing would make either myself or my colleagues on this side of the house happier than to be able to move an amendment such as the one he has proposed, while at the same time be able to say to the people of Canada that we are not going to have to increase old age security taxes. speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, this house and the people of this country should be made aware of the fact that the government and, I regret to say, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, turned down an amendment proposed by the Conservative party in the committee, which would have made it possible to pay $100 per month at age 65 without any increase in taxation.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege. The members of the Progressive Conservative party moved no such amendment in the committee. They moved an entirely different proposition. It was I who moved this amendment and it was that party which voted against it.
