speechtext:
That may be so, Mr. Chairman, and I did not deny that on the first occasion I spoke. However, I repeat that the members of this party did move an amendment which would provide old age pensioners with $100 per month at age 65 as of January 1, 1966, by increasing the Canada pension to the extent of $25. Surely the minister should not now indicate to the house and to the people of this country that such an increase is impossible because the government has to act in a responsible way in so far as the taxpayers and businessmen are concerned. The proposition we put forward would not cost the taxpayers five cents in extra taxes.
The hon. minister asked me at that stage of our committee proceedings whether I would vote for increased taxation in order to pay $100 per month to old age pensioners at age 65. While I do not subscribe to his suggestion that there would be an increase in taxation as a result of the adoption of our proposal-I do not think all my colleagues on this side of the house would go along with me in this regard-I would vote for the increase in taxation which the minister now says would be caused by the implementation of that provision, because he has turned down the opportunity given to him by the proposal made by Conservative members of that committee.
Let me state again that the proposal put forward by the Progressive Conservative party was to grant $100 per month at age 65 without increased taxation, and I think that point must be made clear. It is all very well for the government to create the image with the electorate that it is doing everything possible, but surely they must examine the other side of the coin. This is like suggesting that the government accepts all the credit for
Canada Pension Plan
putting Mr. X in jail, but cannot accept any responsibility for letting him out.
I make these few remarks at this time, Mr. Chairman, so that the people of this country will understand that there was an alternative method of paying $100 per month to that of increasing taxes, as suggested by the minister. I supported that alternative at the time it was proposed in the committee and I am now prepared to support the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, if someone on the other side of this house has the intestinal fortitude to move it as an amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks in connection with the statement made by the minister, in which he mentioned the $800 million odd it would cost to implement the proposal to pay $100 per month at age 65.
Surely the minister is aware that the additional purchasing power placed in the hands of individuals across this country as a result of the increase from $75 to $100 would create sufficient extra business in this country with resulting increases in taxes to offset the $800 million to which he has referred. I do not think the figure he used is a realistic one. As far as we are concerned, we do not accept seriously the claim made by the minister that this increase in benefits would cost $800 million. I believe that the increase would in effect allow the recipients in this country to take advantage of goods and services available, increasing business and employment, and in turn result in increased taxation, which would offset that cost.

Mr. Chairman, after the heartbreaking appeals made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who, once again, thanks to his knowledge of parliamentary procedure, succeeded in putting on the record quite a number of requests on behalf of our older people-I hope nobody will think that they were made only for political reasons- I must say that I do not have the privilege to move an amendment, since that would entail additional expenses for the government; I will not move a subamendment either, but I am convinced that, in spite of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may think, it would not be doing too much for people who lived for several years in a climate of insecurity to change the figure of 100 to 125.

Canada Pension Plan
At this point, I feel it is my duty to point out to the house that our concern differs on at least two points.
Some apply to the study of this clause. Our concern is this. Will the standards set up on a $75 a month basis remain as such for a long time or is an increase possible depending on the price index. Others would prefer to see the increase related to the salary index. Others still are concerned with the tax increase which might follow. As the Minister of National Revenue said earlier, I would certainly prefer to give $100 rather than $75 but it would cost, according to his figures, $821 million extra to meet that payment of $100 a month.
The majority of people are concerned since as a safety measure these words have been added: "an adjustment on the basis of the price index." It is therefore recognized that this is a situation where economists and actuaries are not too sure where we are going.
The price index, the cost of living index or the salaries index do not necessarily comply with a request for price accounting or cost price accounting as concerns salaries.
I hope you are not under the impression that I want to play politics with this clause of the bill. Not too long ago it was claimed on television when bank notes and marks were bandied about that the monetary policies advocated by the Creditistes would constitute the worst danger of runaway inflation in this country.
I am wondering if most of those who talked about clause 120 this afternoon did not stress the danger of inflation, since it is deemed advisable to increase the basic amount of $75 in keeping with the price index.
Some would prefer the wage index basis. Others fear a general tax increase since part IV of the bill and not section IV-because I made a mistake about an hour ago by mentioning section IV instead of part IV and someone succeeded very well in getting around my question.
There are many who recognize that there is really a possibility of inflation under clause 120 as far as the present pension plan is concerned, since reference is made to a basic payment of $75 with a possible increase according to the cost of living index. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) told us that we should adapt ourselves to the needs of the times. He mentioned that some people were in receipt of a basic pension before the existence of television therefore, those people did not have to

buy any t.v. sets at that time but now, one must face those new needs.
Reference could also have been made to the $46 billion production disclosed by the official statistics for 1963; a total production of $46 billion in Canada. When you consider the number of less than $2,000 salaries paid to small wage earners from whom Bill No. C-136 will precisely get a part of that income, I think we should be that much more concerned about the amount of the contribution, because no one was prepared to admit that it was a tax although we were given the privilege to call it a tax, if we wished to, but the minister would not say that it was a tax, he rather pretended that it was a contribution. What will be that contribution in 10 or 20 years from now?
Since inflationary matters are being discussed this afternoon and since there is a fear that the minimum of $75 will not be sufficient to enable old people to make a decent living, I think there should be more concern about what the contribution will be, that contribution which we were allowed to call a tax, even if no one, in government circles, will say it is a tax, although it is one, and mostly a tax on poverty. That part precisely deals with the minimum pension of $75, which is related to the whole tax situation. Now being related to the whole tax situation, it is not a tax on poverty such as the contribution about which there seems to be no concern as to what it will be in 10, 15 or 20 years.
I shall have an opportunity to quote figures concerning this contribution problem during the discussion on clause 1. While the actuaries anticipate that the minimum deduction of 1.8 per cent will be sufficient to accumulate funds up to $8 billion 10 or 20 year hence, I will prove the mathematical impossibility of these estimates and I shall prove that it will be necessary to increase the contributions of the small wage earners who already have hardly enough to live on.
This part of Bill No. C-136 does not worry them. They are not wondering what will be the contributions and what part of the salary will be withheld when 4 per cent of the salary of the employee and 4 per cent, being the employer's share, will have to be paid.
I wished to point out that it is not the monetary theories advocated by us for many years but the financial policies of the Liberals and the Conservatives that are responsible for this inflationary system.

Mr. Chairman, this clause as amended provides a pension of $75 a month. We in this party feel that it should be $100 a month and I should like to speak on this question. Let me take this opportunity, first of all, to express my general endorsation of the income related provisions of this plan. As it has been said in the house, I think this plan is of far reaching and historic importance. However, I think it is only half a program, and that it is necessary to complete the program by the provision of $100 a month at age 65.
Since this is my first opportunity of addressing the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I should like to take a moment before going into the other matters publicly to express my appreciation of her and her department for the excellent attention which have been given to the problems in my riding. I am sure that my constituents are very grateful for the efficient manner in which she has dealt with these problems.
Now, having said that-
Oh, oh.

It does not take long to learn here. In the speech of the minister the other day she said that as the plan now stood it was both fair and practical. I submit that this plan, unless it provides $100 a month at age 65, for a large segment of the population of Canada will be neither fair nor practical. It will not be fair to the present generation of our elderly people. They could very well become the forgotten generation, while we are concerned with making plans for the distant future.
This is a generation which probably has worked harder than any other generation in the history of Canada will ever have to work. This is a generation which has survived two wars. I am trying not to get emotional about this, there is no point in that; I am merely pointing out that this is a generation which has gone through probably the worst economic conditions of recent times. This is a generation which was taxed to provide most of the social capital we now have in Canada. This is a generation that financed our present prosperity, that paid for our roads, hospitals and schools. It contributed to the financing of municipal services.
As someone who has recently come from a municipal council, I can state-and I am sure all hon. members here are aware of this- that there are many people who, after having saved for an entire lifetime to own a home of
Canada Pension Plan
their own, are now finding it almost impossible to meet the cost of maintaining that home. These people come to their local council and ask them to find some way of reducing the taxation on their homes so that they might continue to own something they have worked a lifetime to build. We all know that councils cannot do this sort of thing; they cannot reduce taxation for one person and not for another. Not only that, but they need this type of taxation in order to provide the services which are absolutely necessary today.
When I served on a council I was quite aware of this problem and I am still aware of it. The problem can be met only at this level; and this is why I am appealing to the government to endorse the suggestion that the pension be increased to $100 a month because this is the only way we can help the older people of the country. I think we have an obligation in this regard.
Another matter I want to raise is that I do not think this bill is being fair to the consciences of the young people of Canada. We hear a great deal about mortgaging our future, but I do not think it is the young people who are mortgaging their futures. It is the old people who have mortgaged their future for the sake of the young. I think that the young owe this generation something, and if we must have higher taxes, then let us have higher taxes to meet this cost. We have a deep and abiding obligation to the older people of this nation.
I also do not feel that the provisions of the bill are fair to the economy. In this regard I hope the Minister of National Revenue will excuse me if I seem presumptuous-I have that presumption which comes only to the younger members-but I should like to make a suggestion about how he might be able to find the magnificent amount of $820 million about which he talks so blithely. I think that unless we are prepared to find some way of putting money into the consumer sector of the economy when we are withdrawing almost a billion dollars a year from the Canada pension fund for capital investment, we might find ourselves in very serious difficulty. The economy is going to need consumer dollars. We are not going to get these consumer dollars by withdrawing almost a billion dollars a year for capital investment, worthwhile as capital and social investment may be. I feel it is equally necessary for the government to

Canada Pension Plan
recognize that consumption must be maintained. Unless we are prepared to assure the consumer more income and social justice, there will be nothing practical or fair about the Canada pension plan.
I have no doubt that there are other ways of doing it. There have been rumours that taxes will be cut. I say here today that if the government cuts taxes, if the government feels the economy of this nation is strong enough to cut taxes but does not give an increase in the old age pension, then the government will have a lot to answer for to the Canadian people. The refusal of the government to implement old age security at age 65 will indicate something else. It will indicate that the government has no confidence in its ability to achieve the growth rates outlined as necessary in the report of the economic council of Canada. The report indicates a number of things. It indicates that our national output must be up 45 per cent by 1970; that as many new jobs must be created in the next seven years as were created in the last 14 years; that unemployment must be down again to 3 per cent. We need a growth rate of 5.5 per cent of the gross national product every year until 1970. Employment will have to rise at an annual average rate of 3.1 per cent and productivity will have to be increased.
If the government meets these objectives, which I feel it must meet, there can be no excuse for saying that we cannot afford to pay $100 at age 65. I think it must meet these objectives. It must show its confidence that it will meet these objectives by giving $100 per month at age 65 to our people now. I do not believe there is anything that will establish that degree of confidence in this nation as will such a measure at this time. I feel these goals must be met, without question, if Canada is to reach its potential. A government, committed to such a growth pattern should not tell the people of Canada that $100 per month is not within the capabilities of this nation. The increased tax revenues resulting from this increased growth could easily handle this obligation to benefit our labouring people.
If this growth takes place, income taxes under the present rate provisions may be expected to more than double by 1970. This will be the greatest source of revenue of all and will make it possible, in my opinion, to finance the sort of thing about which we are talking. This infusion of additional money into the economy should go a long way toward stimulating the economy to the objective in 1970.

The Minister of National Revenue, when he talks about $820 million, uses a figure that boggles the imagination. However, when he uses that figure he does not indicate whether or not there are compensating savings if the old age pension is instituted at these rates.
I had intended to put a number of questions on the order paper, but since this debate has been proceeding so quickly I think I might ask these questions of the minister now. I should like to know how much money will be saved when the minister takes into consideration the moneys that are now being paid to people over 65, or who are 70 and who are in receipt of a pension from the disabled persons allowance. I should like to know whether or not administrative costs could be saved by having a universal old age pension. I believe the minister has answered this question, but I should like to know what will be saved in terms of old age assistance, now that I understand the additional taxes from the 3-3-4 formula will be sufficient to raise $278 million by 1970. In view of these increased revenues, no change in taxation will be needed in order to bring the pensionable age down to 65. I should like to know how much money would be saved if a worth-while pension were given at age 65? How much money would be saved from the unemployment insurance fund?
There are people collecting money from the unemployment insurance fund, who are registered with that fund, and who are not unemployed but who are unemployable. They are being financed out of the fund. The Gill commission report has indicated that the fund should be protected. When we are talking about money, I think we should recognize that the government is bearing the entire cost of the administration of that fund. It is subsidizing it to the tune of $60 million a year, and it is using the fund as a social insurance agency. This is an unemployment insurance fund, and the government should accept the recommendations of the Gill commission. It should put the fund on an insurance basis and should release some of that money for old age assistance, where it properly belongs.
There are other programs in which the government is presently involved with the provinces and with the municipalities. There is a hodge-podge of social service programs in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please; the committee has been listening with great interest to the speech being made by the hon.

member. However, I have some doubt as to whether he is not now embarking upon a path that will lead him farther away from the question we should be considering, and which is limited to clause 120 of this bill. I would ask him to keep in mind that, according to the rules, he should limit himself to the subject matter before the committee which, at the moment, is clause 120 of this bill.

May I speak to the point of order? May I draw attention to the fact that the whole discussion revolves around whether or not the pension should be raised to $100 per month. The Minister of National Revenue has pointed out to the committee that this would mean an increased cost of $820 million, and really asked the committee where he is to get it. The hon. member is now in the process of pointing out how this money can be procured, and how savings can be accomplished in order to carry out the suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
It seems to me that if the Minister of National Revenue is going to be allowed to oppose the suggestion of $100 per month on the ground it is going to cost a large sum of money, then any member of the committee is in order in discussing how this money can be raised, or saved by forgoing some other program.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. On the point of order raised by the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam, I am afraid I cannot agree with the suggestion he is making now. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself recognized the amendment to which he referred would be out of order. If the amendment would be out of order, a debate on that amendment would be equally out of order. I allowed the hon. member for Waterloo South quite a bit of latitude. I do not intend to restrict him unduly, but I think it is the duty of the Chair to caution him that he has to keep in mind standing order 59(2).

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Surely, the whole question before the committee is the amount of the pension, and whether or not it is adequate, whether or not it should be adjusted. The ministers have spoken on that subject; others should be allowed to do likewise.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, I should like to say that what we are talking about is whether or not the amount is adequate or inadequate. We are not discussing an amendment. We are dis-
Canada Pension Plan
cussing whether or not this amount is adequate. The hon. member is trying to prove it is inadequate and, second, pointing out that the minister's argument that money cannot be procured is fallacious.
Order.
There is no cause calling order. You are not going to push this through by yelling order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On the point of order, I was following with intense interest the suggestion being made by the hon. member for Waterloo South, who was presenting a very good argument. It is not an amendment which is in front of us. It is just a suggestion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that if the government were alive it would move an amendment along the lines he has suggested. The proposal before the committee is that there should be a higher pension, and the hon. member is suggesting ways and means by which it could be made available.

Mr. Chairman, I shall try to address my remarks as pertinently as I can to the subject. I have a further number of questions I would like to direct to the Minister of National Revenue, and I feel this question of costs is very pertinent to the whole matter. That is the great argument involved. I do not think anyone would argue for one minute that there is a single person in this chamber who would be against increasing old age pensions. The core of the entire argument is the question of whether the nation can afford such a cost, and it is on that question I would like to speak.
I would like to ask the minister whether he has made a study to see what increases in revenues would accrue through the increased activity of such a sum of money being pumped into the economy? I would like to ask him whether he has made a study to see what stimulative effect this would have on taxes? I would like to ask him has he made a study to see to what extent unemployment would be reduced by such an infusion of consumer spending?
When he was speaking the other day the minister said there was a question of priorities. He pointed out that we have many problems in Canada-that we have problems in education that have to be met; that we have problems in the development of other forms of social capital; that we have problems of medical services that have to be met-and the minister felt these problems and priorities had to be taken into consideration. However,

Canada Pension Plan
I feel this is a priority of such a nature that it must be met first, and not only will the meeting of this priority take care of a social problem but it will also help the whole economy.
When the minister talks about priorities does he feel the $35 million loss suffered by the Post Office Department on second class mail is more important than paying old age pensions? I wonder whether the Minister of Industry feels that the $50 million he is giving to the automotive companies of Canada is far more important than money given to the old age pensioners of Canada. I understand he is doing this in the interests of employment, but I think more employment would accrue to the nation through old people getting money to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If the hon. member would not mind my interrupting, he is one of the newest members here, and although this is not a maiden speech it is very nearly one- and an excellent one. Does he not remember that a few months before he ran for parliament the House of Commons raised old age pensions $10 a month at an expenditure of an extra $116 million per year? It is not fair to single out one $50 million sum and say nothing is being done when, in a sense, this government since coming to power has raised something like $250 million extra for pensions.

I recognize the merit of the statement made by the minister and I do not for one minute say nothing has been done; but I do say that not enough has been done, and not enough has been done in a courageous way. Has this country ever gone broke or suffered economically by giving money to old people? There has never been an instance in Canada when pensions were raised that the increase was not followed by a period of relative prosperity. No one has tied down increases in old age pensions to recessions in Canada. I would like to raise one more question, and then I will leave the restless troops to their voting.
We talk about national unity in this country. We use very grand phrases and everybody is in favour of national unity; yet over and over again we see areas in which the federal government is not prepared to move boldly and decisively and give leadership to the nation. The government has this opportunity now. It has the opportunity to recognize the gulf and the gaps that exist in income in Canada. It has an opportunity to do something about this at the national level,

and if the federal government will not act the provincial governments will have no alternative but to take over authority and responsibility.
The farmers in Canada are getting a less and less share of the national wealth as the years go by. Yes, we have done many things. We have tried many things to help the farmers in Canada, but this is one of the few areas in national policy where a pension at a certain age can go to every Canadian, whether he be a farmer or industrial worker. This is one area in which we can close the gap in earnings between the farmer and the industrial worker. We have the opportunity to do it and I think we should do it.
I would like to point out that the province of Quebec is getting 87 per cent of the average national income it might, whereas the province of Ontario is getting 117 per cent. If we talk about national unity, if we talk about one nation, if we talk about bringing people together, what better way of closing the economic gap than having the government provide these pensions? These pensions go to farmers, industrial workers, French Canadians, ethnic Canadians and English Canadians. They can go a long way to solving some of the problems we have today.
If we have a problem today in confederation, if there are arguments between the provinces and the federal government, I think to some extent we have brought these on ourselves. It is time we were aggressive and took the proper kind of steps to indicate to the provinces that we are willing to assist in overcoming these problems.

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks made by the hon. member who spoke before me in connection with the old age pension set at $100 a month, I should say that he was right in referring, particularly at the conclusion of his remarks, to the fact that, to the extent to which we would assist the older people in our country, these people would contribute not only to the economic stability, but also to the unity which is endangered here at the moment, precisely by using the credit at their disposal to improve our Canadian economy.

The party to my immediate right has urged the principle that old age pensions be raised to a minimum of $100 a month. I agree with that proposal put forward by the hon. mem-

ber for Winnipeg North Centre, but I think the hon. member is still far too modest in his demand. The minister has pointed out that to pay such a pension would cost $820 million. In my view $100 would certainly meet the needs of senior citizens to some extent, but it would be more realistic and more practical to increase it to $125.
I wish to explain briefly how we might raise this extra $25 for each senior citizen in our country. It was lately announced that the Canadian government had advanced $200 million interest free in order to support the pound sterling in the United Kingdom. This money came from the Bank of Canada. Why not guarantee $25 more for our old age pensioners by using the Bank of Canada in the same way as we guaranteed the pound sterling? Would this cause inflation? The answer, Mr. Chairman, is no. Neither would it increase taxation, though it would certainly increase the purchasing power in the hands of the people of this country.
The older generation is, at this moment, helping the younger citizens of our country; they have their interests at heart. Believe me, this extra money will not be saved, it will be put back into the economy; it will stimulate the economy and help close the gap between the purchasing power of our citizens and the production available to them. Let us provide not only the $100 a month suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Let us make available this extra $25 and finance it, not by going into the pockets of the taxpayers but by taking advantage of the presence of the Bank of Canada. It would be more practical and more realistic in accordance with today's needs to think in terms of $125. We all know that the cost of living is no less for senior citizens than it is for the young. Indeed, the cost of medical care is often greater for old people than it is for younger people. I think the hon. member for Mercier would be proud to announce that in addition to $100 old age pensioners were to be given $25 more, based on our capacity to produce, and guaranteed by the Bank of Canada. I urge the minister to consider this suggestion because it is one which will commend itself I believe not only to members of this committee but to everyone in the country.

The proposal has been made to the government that old age pensions should be increased to $100 a month effective immediately, thus eliminating the need for clause 121 in this amendment to the Old Age Security Act.
Canada Pension Plan
The Minister of National Revenue has stated this proposal would cost more than $800 million a year and that it is not financially feasible. I would ask him whether as an alternative the government would not consider raising old age pensions at the rate of $5 per month per year to coincide with the reduction of the minimum age requirement one year at a time, until the old age pension had reached $100 a month. This would deal with the obvious gap which has been created by the bill now under consideration.

It was not my intention to speak on this clause until the Minister of National Revenue made the observations he did, telling the committee we could not afford the proposal for increased pension rates. Spokesmen for the Liberal party have always taken this line.
The minister gave us the figure of $800 million which, I take it, is the total cost involved in providing $100 at the age of 65, without taking into consideration the savings which would result from the elimination of the Old Age Assistance Act and a number of other sizeable pieces of legislation under which money is paid to people between the ages of 65 and 70. This is not an unusual attitude to take; the Liberals have been adopting it for a long time. I was interested to read a statement made in the house by the senior member of this party, the hon. member for Kootenay West, on March 30, 1950. Old age security measures were being discussed at that time and government spokesmen were putting forward the same arguments as they have been putting forward today. My hon. friend said:
These are several approaches to the question of old age security. In the main we find there are two plans put forward by members of the house and by people outside the house. The first is some scheme of compulsory contributions based on the insurance principle. The second is the payment of old age pensions from taxation based on ability to pay.
Then he went on to say he was in favour of the second of these approaches.
Members of the party to which I belong have always been of the opinion that legislation which provides benefits for the Canadian people needs to be paid for. We also believe that old age security is the responsibility of all the people and that if we are to pay higher old age pensions taxes may have to be raised. But have we not been dishonest, politically, with the old age pensioners for a number of years, now? I have run in four elections and one of the major planks in the

Canada Pension Plan
platform of every political party has always been an increase in old age pensions. We have heard Liberal party spokesmen saying in the past: We cannot give an increase; the economy of the nation will not stand it. We all remember the $6 which they said represented their limit. Well, we saw another political party raise that figure, and since then the Liberal party has raised it again. On all these occasions the money has been found.
There is one factor which in my opinion is wrong with the whole pension plan and with Liberal thinking on pensions in general. They have never been willing to tax across the board; they have been willing to tax only one segment of the population. They have never been willing to remove the $3,000 limit on the old age security tax. Perhaps the minister would tell me why persons earning more than $3,000 do not have to make a fair and reasonable contribution to the old age security system we now have. I was of the opinion that the government would need to reach a decision about revising the age of eligibility. If a general election should come, mark my words, the Liberal party will promise the old age pensioner an increase immediately after the next election, no matter whether it is held this year or next year. They will make those promises, and make them regardless of the position of the treasury. But they have given the undertaking now in a fair, reasonable and honest way to the Canadian public; they are going to use it again as an election issue.
I decided that I wanted to know from my constituents whether they were interested in reducing the age at which the old age pensioner would receive his pension, and also if they favoured increasing that old age pension, and I also added, "Even if this will cost more money and increase your taxes, are you in favour of reducing the age to 65 and increasing the amount of the old age pension?" I have received from my constituents, on a mailing list, what I consider to be a reasonable and fair sampling of opinion in my riding. I am quite happy to say on behalf of those people that 87 per cent of them said yes, they were in favour of even increasing taxes to provide an increase in the old age pension and a decrease in the age at which people would receive a pension. This means that only 13 per cent of the people in Timis-kaming are of the same opinion as the Minister of National Revenue, namely that this country cannot, will not and is not prepared

to raise taxes to support an increase in the old age pension and a decrease in the age.
The Prime Minister is in the chamber at the present time. I am sure he is not just here for fun, and certainly he is not here just to listen to me. I am quite sure he has been informed of the wish and aspirations of the member for Winnipeg North Centre that one of the ministers should consider moving the amendment that we, by the rules of this house, are not permitted to move. I would hope that the Prime Minister would discuss during the supper hour the possibilities of giving the committee the opportunity of making the decision as to whether they are willing to endorse the proposition that has been outlined by the member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I know there are many members of the Liberal party-I am sure this is true-who faced the problem long ago of deciding that the old age pensioners in this country are not the responsibility of their families but are the responsibility of the nation. I think the speech made by the hon. member for Waterloo South was an excellent one, and I believe that the proposals he made are ones that the government must consider; because I think it is entirely up to the people of Canada, and their elected representatives are the people who have to decide in regard to this question. They should have the opportunity to decide whether or not this is how we Canadians want to spend our money. I am sure there are few members in this house who would not be willing to go back to their ridings and say, "Yes, we have raised the old age pension and we have brought the age of retirement into line with the practices in industry and employment in this nation. We have decided to pay for it out of general revenues and the taxation of this nation, because we believe that the people who have made the contribution to this country that has been made by those who are now reaching retirement age are the responsibility of the economy of the country". We should all be pledged to raise the gross national product to an extent where it can carry in decency the old aged people of this nation.
The Minister of National Revenue has pointed out that this will cost $820 million. I think he will agree with me that this is not the actual cost to the Canadian public. I believe he will agree that there are two classes of old age pensioner. The hon. member for Kootenay West, when speaking on this subject in 1950, pointed out that there are two classes of old age pensioner; there are those

speechtext:
who cannot afford to keep themselves in retirement, and there are those who can afford it. At that time he pointed out that those who could afford a retirement fund to provide for themselves amounted to probably less than 15 per cent of the retired public. But I think the minister will also agree that in regard to the other 85 per cent who will be drawing old age security, this money is not like other moneys paid in taxes; it is not like money you spend on national defence; it is not like money you spend in many, many other ways-but by putting it into the social security of our nation and the social capital of our nation the government gets this money back very rapidly. There have been some who have said this money probably only passes through five stages before it goes back to the federal treasury. This is money that has to be spent. It meets the needs of the economy; it meets the needs of a people, and for this reason it goes back very rapidly into the economy.
I think the minister could quite easily come back before the committee after supper and inform us that the amount is not $820 million but that the total cost in real expenditure might amount to $200 million. The minister shakes his head, but I am saying that the amount of $820 million that he speaks of is not the correct figure of the expenditures we are going to make. It is a figure that is exact in so far as it goes, but it is not the true picture of the cost to the Canadian public. It is a figure that can be arrived at for total cost, but cost in regard to social security is not actually a total cost but only a partial cost, because this makes up the fabric of our economy. Moneys that are eventually returned to the federal government in connection with social security are not a total cost.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to embark upon a long, detailed discussion of how money returns to the federal treasury and what becomes of it, but I believe the minister can legitimately say that this is not the amount it will cost the public. I am also sure that the 87 per cent of the people in my riding who are willing to make the necessary contribution to raise this pension to $100 are representative of the people across Canada, and that if a national poll were conducted it would produce figures very similar to those I have used.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee has before it for consideration an amendment to clause 120 as proposed by the Minister of National Revenue.
Shall the amendment carry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to discuss the proposal presented to us by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The hon. member's proposal is very interesting, but I for one cannot support it. Does the hon. member really think we can pile tax upon tax on the taxpayers of this country ad infinitum? The hon. member introduced this proposal during the January-February sittings of the special joint committee on the Canada pension plan, and he took some pains this evening to point out that his party voted for the proposal at that time. Perhaps he took more pains to point out that the rest of us did not vote for the proposal, and by doing so I suppose he is suggesting that we are not particularly concerned with the welfare of those individuals of this country who are to receive pensions. I am sure all parties, not just the one to which I belong, would deny that suggestion categorically. We are just as concerned with this group of individuals as his party is, the only difference being that we would attempt to look after them in a different way.
The party to which I belong took some pains at the sittings of the special joint committee to prepare what we thought were responsible and intelligent proposals embodying methods of obtaining larger pensions for pensioners. The proposal we made at that time was a more responsible proposal than that suggested by the hon. member, because the money required by our proposal was to come from the Canada pension plan. I am quite sure that the necessary money could have been found in that way.

Canada Pension Plan
Very large funds are being set up by the Canada pension plan. It is my view that a great deal of the money is being provided to assist provincial governments in socially acceptable works which they wish to carry out. As I have pointed out in respect of this subject, it is my feeling that the provincial governments can find this money in other ways, because they have experienced little or no difficulty so far in this regard. The hon. member has pointed out that we do not seem to be very concerned with the aged of this country. Perhaps it will be of interest to note that when in office the party to which I belong raised old age payments on two occasions. Last October this same party provided the lead which resulted in an increase in payments to $75.
During the sittings of the special committee members of the Progressive Conservative party made suggestions which would have obtained for all retired Canadians a pension of $100 per month. The specific suggestion to which I have referred embodied ways of carrying out increased pension payments in a much more responsible way than could be envisaged in the proposal put forward by the New Democratic party.
Perhaps at this time I may be allowed to report what we actually did suggest at those committee meetings, and this proposed amendment is to be found in the last volume of the proceedings and evidence of that committee, at page 2056, and reads as follows:
Therefore to correct these gross omissions and inequities the committee recommends that consideration be given to amending Bill C-136 to provide that:
(a)	all persons over age 70 receiving old age security benefits shall receive an additional uniform flat amount of not more than $25 a month to be paid from the Canada pension plan fund when the first benefit payments are made from the fund.
I need hardly state at this point, since these new suggestions have been made that we begin the pension payments at age 69 and then down to 68, 67, 66 until finally we reach 65, that our recommendations would now include the additional $25 per month during this whole age period.
Then paragraph (b) of that amendment is as follows:
(b)	all persons between 65 and 70 who meet a retirement test and who elect to draw the actuarially reduced old age security payment shall receive an additional uniform flat amount of not more than $25 a month to be paid from the Canada pension plan fund when the first benefit payments are made from the fund.

I think that supports the statement I have just made, that we obviously intended to include those who will now receive payments from age 65 and onwards. We also suggested how the money could be found to accomplish this purpose.
I am intrigued by the comment of the Minister of National Revenue to the effect that the increase from $75 to $100 per month would require an additional $800 million and some odd in the first year. I must confess that I find this figure difficult to reconcile with the information we received to the effect that the increase of $10 in the old age security last fall only cost $116 million. Perhaps I am mistaken in that regard, but that is my impression of the information we received.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps if the hon. member will allow me, I should give some explanation at this point. The proposal made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is that the additional $25 be paid from age 65 on, which will require much greater expenditure than an increase of $10 per month payable to those over age 70.

I thank the hon. minister for his explanation, but I think I should point out that the increase of $25 per month which we suggested, using the same calculation as was used in arriving at the $116 million in reference to the $10 per month increase, would only amount to $290 million. I am sure that the funds created by the Canada pension plan could easily carry that increase. I am sure we are all aware that there will be very large funds created by the Canada pension plan.
With those few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I think I have emphasized the fact that the party to which I belong is just as concerned with that group of retiring individuals in this country as is any other party. This group has done its share not only during committee proceedings but during the proceedings of this house to indicate to the public that we are so concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I was a little concerned when the committee began its sitting at eight o'clock that we were going to be in a position of having to agree to the passage of this clause in its present form, because it appeared that there would be no one on the ministerial benches except the tight-fisted Minister of National Revenue who could possibly rise to the occasion to reply to some of the suggestions which have been

advanced. In fact, I was quite concerned earlier this afternoon when I felt sure in my own mind that our present Secretary of State for External Affairs, in view of his long held former portfolio as minister of national health and welfare, was sitting on the edge of his seat to move the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. But 1 noticed how abruptly the Minister of National Revenue, in his hardhearted way, jumped to his feet to cut him off from that opportunity.
However, my hopes and anticipations have been rising steadily during the last few minutes because I notice that not only has the Secretary of State for External Affairs come back into the house but the Prime Minister has come into the house with a very amiable smile on his face, and I am sure that he has by now given consideration to the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming just before six o'clock. I am sure we would all be very pleased and highly honoured if the Prime Minister himself would rise to put forward the proposal from the treasury benches which was suggested so eloquently earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the amendment
carry?

Mr. Chairman, before this item carries I think it is important that we should take a little further look at it than we have today. The government seems determined not to increase beyond $75 a month the basic pension allowable under the pension plan. But there are more than only the bare essentials involved in the question whether it should be $75 or $100. After all, by virtue of its name of the Canada pension plan a certain impression has been created in the minds of the people of Canada, and as I look at the plan there are vast numbers who will benefit very little from the plan as presently constituted. From the questions about it coming to me through the mails at the present time I believe many people are wondering just what benefit the plan may be to them. I feel that at this time all we are extending to those who are employable and employed is the benefit of-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I bring to the hon. member's attention that we are not discussing the general principle of the bill at this time. Neither are we at the resolution stage, second reading or on clause 1. We are discussing clause 120, specifically an amendment to clause 120, which is part of part IV 20220-783
Canada Pension Plan
of the bill dealing with amendments to the Old Age Security Act. I would suggest to the hon. member that he restrict his consideration to this aspect of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, this is what I was getting down to in my introductory comments. I have the particular clause before me and I am well aware of what is before the committee at the present time.
I thought this afternoon that the hon. member for Waterloo South stated very clearly the choice which is before parliament at this time. I was a little surprised that the Minister of National Revenue indicated the proposal made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would cost $815 million. I think that when these other matters which were mentioned today are taken into consideration the actual cost to the treasury of this country would be much less than the $815 million suggested by the Minister of National Revenue.
I was interested to see this afternoon and again this evening a number of the members of cabinet who have not been in their places too often during this debate in the committee. As I look at them tonight I cannot help but feel that there is a division among the cabinet members on this particular matter. I hope that before the vote on this particular amendment is taken they may be able to resolve that division among themselves and come out in favour of the figure included in the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I have nothing further to say at this time, except that even at $100 as a basic pension we would not be paying too much to those receiving old age security.

Mr. Chairman, clause 121 reads, in part, as follows:
The said act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 3 thereof, the following section: "A. (1} The basic amount of the monthly flat-rate pension that may be paid to any person. ..is seventy five dollars.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, that provision of part IV of the bill before us is not doing justice to the Canadian people, to the people we are representing here in the House of Commons.
A few weeks ago when the Prime,Minister (Mr. Pearson) announced that the old age pension would be increased to $75 a month at 65 years without any means test in 1970, I stated then that such a pension would not be enough to permit our fellow citizens, those

Canada Pension Plan
we are representing in this house, to meet their obligations adequately.
Subsection 2 of section 3A states:
Where, either before or after the coming into force of this section, any pension has been authorized to be paid to a person, the amount of such pension shall be adjusted annually, in such manner as may be prescribed by regulation, so that the amount that may be paid to such person for a month in any year after 1967 is the product obtained by multiplying-
Then, you have to multiply. I continue:
(a)	the basic amount of such pension, by
(b)	the ratio that the pension index for that year bears to the pension index for the year 1967.
I think that even the most experienced lawyers in the house are lost in conjecture. Nobody understands. I see that my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) seems to agree entirely with me. Lawyers themselves do not understand anything, not only about section 120, clause 3A, paragraphs (1) and (2), subparagraphs (a) and (b), but about the whole bill.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is a charming woman, does not understand anything either; she nods in assent and she is the one who is introducing this bill.
Mr. Chairman, why waste our time with clauses worded in this fashion, when nobody understands anything about them?
I said time and again that it was not the intention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister of Canada to grant a pension to those who had reached the age of 65, but to collect within 10 years billions of dollars from people who are presently working and then have our children pay for the pension we will receive when we reach the age of 65 or 70.
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of clause 120 of Bill No. C-136 is not so much the establishment of a pension fund as the collection of new taxes for the government which today is administering our country. But this motive is hidden under the pretext that we are assisting people at the age of 65.
I claim that this clause, like the other clauses of Bill No. C-136, parts I, II, III or IV, constitute another mode of taxation which they do not want to call as such. However, under the pretence that a pension will be paid 40 years hence, funds are gathered to finance the deficit of the present government.
Furthermore, clause 120 provides that the pension index is the same as that stipulated in clause 20 of the Canada pension plan. Therefore, from clause 120, one must revert
[Mr. Caouette.l
to clause 20 to see what is the pension index mentioned therein. The pension index is figured for any year, as provided for in the said section.
As I said a while ago, lawyers cannot understand this. The government does not know what to do with its bill.
I see that the Minister of National Revenue finds this funny because he undoubtedly needs additional funds to administer his scheme.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare also is laughing.
However, Mr. Chairman, we are not at all ready to agree to a new tax levy which is being called old age pensions instead of additional tax. At that time we will not get our money back, we will be paid a meagre pension out of the money that will be collected from our own children.
I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has no children and probably will never have any. However, we have children and, 20 or 30 years from now we do not want them to have to pay us a pension that the minister is trying to get out of us today to make up in fact the federal government's deficit.

On clause 121-Exception where applicant over 65 years when application received.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move that clause No. 121 be amended to read as follows:
Section 4 of the said act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after subsection (1) thereof, the following subsection:
"(la) Notwithstanding subsection (1), where a person who has applied to receive a pension attained the age of 65 years before the day on which the application was received, the approval of the application may be effective as of such earlier day, not before the later of
(a)	a day one year before the day on which the application was received, or
(b)	the day on which the applicant attained the age of 65 years,
as may be prescribed by regulation."
This clause is adapted from section 122 of part IV. It provides for the approval of an application for pension as of an earlier date than the date on which the application was received in those cases where there has been some delay in making application after the applicant has attained the age of 65 years.
It will be noted that section 122, which provides for the progressive reduction in age will govern the application of this section during the five transitional years that are provided.

This provision will permit the payment of a pension benefit where there has been some delay in making the application for benefit up to a period of one year. This is particularly helpful in the case of older persons who may find when obtaining evidence of age that they are older than they had realized.

I should like to say a word on this clause. I am heartily in accord with the intent behind this provision in that it does make it possible for some elderly persons who have, by error or omission, neglected to file an application in time to receive old age security upon actually attaining the age required. I have many times had the experience of individuals who, for one reason or another, found that they were one year older than they thought they were. As a consequence, they missed out a year's old age security. 1 have known it, upon occasion, to be more than one year. However, I do not quarrel with the idea of making this provision retroactive one year. I am not prepared to say it should be two years. However, I do remember one particular instance in which there were three people from the same city in Canada who found out they had missed their old age security by two years. I can only say that this does fill a need in connection with this legislation and we are heartily in accord with it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I too should like to say a word about this provision. We welcome this amendment to the Old Age Security Act which is provided by clause 121 of this bill. As the Minister of National Revenue has pointed out, the new clause 121 does precisely what the former clause 122 did, only it takes account of the new eligible age of 65. In my experience, which is no doubt similar to that of the hon. member for Perth, this will cover the person who discovers he is older than he thought he was and in such a case now suffers the loss of a year's pension.
Is clause 121 worded in such a way as to take care of people who qualify for the pension at 69, 68 or 67? Former clause 122 specified age 70, and this new clause specifies at age 65. If the bill goes through in its present form, what about a person in 1966 who could have qualified for the pension because he was 69 but did not know it at that time? My concern is that the clause as printed seems to refer so precisely to age 65.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The hon. member will remember that last summer when dealing with
Canada Pension Plan
youth allowances this was one of the things we introduced in that program. It was a new program and it was felt a lot of people would not know about it. It only covered a two year period and so we included a provision whereby people might collect allowances for a year back, no matter how late they applied.
This question has been raised a number of times in respect to old age security. Indeed I as minister have found it a difficult thing to deal with when people, through error, have not known about their age and have applied too late. Sometimes they have lost a month or two and the minister has had no discretion to do anything about it. When the director of old age security checked back through cases on file, he found most would be covered if in effect a year's grace were given so that anyone who had reached almost the age of 71, and through loss of birth records found he was a year older than he thought, would be able to collect back pension payments.
Accordingly, when the decision was made that one should be able to get the flat rate pension at 65, going down each year as provided in clause 122, it was conceded that the same right should be given to everyone. Many people might be out of the country and so would not hear of this new scheme, and we do not want Canadians to lose any part of these pensions simply because they have not heard of them. To placate the fears of my hon. friend, the clause is written so that persons whose birthday brings them to age 65, even if they go almost a year beyond that, will be able to apply and have the pension as of that date.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: My concern is with the interim period. I am concerned about the years during which the eligibility age is coming down a year at a time. This clause makes provision for those who have attained 65 without knowing it; but what about the person who, next year, attains 69 without knowing it? Does this clause cover such a situation, or is it covered by some regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As of the date they are entitled their rights crystallize, and for the next year, even though they do not know they are entitled, they will be able to collect back to a year before, to the time their rights crystallized.

Mr. Chairman, I merely wish to ask the minister a question.

Canada Pension Plan
Did not the minister receive a few moments ago, from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) a draft amendment to the effect that pensions should be paid at age 65 without any test or discrimination whatever, immediately and not in 1970?
I am told that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is anxious to see the pension plan approved.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to a discussion that took place in committee this afternoon concerning clause 120? The amendment he has in mind was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with regard to clause 120 and not clause 121.

Mr. Chairman, you tell me that the amendment was moved when clause 120 was under consideration. Clause 121 reads as follows:
(la) Notwithstanding subsection (1). where a person who has applied to receive a pension attained the age of 70 years before the day on which the application was received,
I think that my remarks are in order, because I am now reading clause 121 which stipulates:
___the approval of the application may be effective as of such earlier day, not before the later of-
Now, which date is as of such earlier day, not before the later?
Imagine how this clause is likely to enlighten the Canadian people as a whole.
I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare burst out laughing on hearing this sentence from clause 121.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am sorry but I must interrupt. I do not know to whom my friend was referring. I was not laughing. My parliamentary secretary asked to speak to me and I turned to speak to him but I was not laughing at anything my hon. friend or anyone else said.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister should be listening to the member who has the floor, not to another minister from the cabinet who does not even know what he is talking about when he talks about this pension plan on any clause.
Order.
I hear my hon. friend from Red Deer say order. He should have been told order in Ethiopia, when he was there a few weeks ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend may I say that, much as he deserves it, my parliamentary secretary is not yet a member of the cabinet.

No, it was not the parliamentary secretary. It was another minister, and a similar one to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

Mr. Chairman, this clause is fairly complete. I understood that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-he is probably one of the few in his group to urge the passing of this pension plan-had moved an amendment, and you tell me that it was on clause 120. That amendment could be applied to clause 121 in order to ask the government to apply the pension plan or to provide for the old age pension without a means test at 65 years, and that is what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre requests so tenaciously.
His amendment has not yet been put to a vote, I believe, and is still valid at this time.
At any rate, I should like the Minister of National Health and Welfare to tell us whether it is true that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has sent her an amendment providing for the payment of a pension to any person of age 65 under this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I have to get rid of all waste paper at every meal break to leave room for the next.

I think this is a good amendment. If I understand it correctly, the proposal means that should any person apply late, that is, after he is eligible, he would be entitled to retroactive payment for a period up to one year. This is true for the whole five years of the transitional period from 70 years down to 65 years. If it is finally established that an applicant could have been eligible for more than a year from the date of approval, however, he will only be paid on a retroactive basis in respect of one year. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is correct.

I have a question for the minister with regard to this proposed amendment. Does it apply to people who are now 70 years of age, or older? Will it apply as soon as this bill becomes effective? It has come to my knowledge that a certain individual for reasons known only to himself failed to make an application for old age

pension until a month ago, although he is now 80 years of age. Will this new provision take care of his case and can he recover a year's payments in arrears when this legislation is proclaimed?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: From whatever date it becomes effective. The bill provides for regulations and under these regulations provision will be made that an individual-in this case he is 80 years of age, and he will be, say, 81 when the bill becomes effective- will be able to draw retroactive benefits in respect of one year. From time to time we are confronted by these late applications. It is not so often the man who is late in applying as it is the woman who is inclined to be ashamed of her age-a married woman, perhaps, who has not made it clear to her husband that she is entitled to a pension. The intention here is that every person shall be able to collect up to a year's pension retroactively, provided he or she is qualified to do so, and I am informed by the director of old age security that this provision will cover most of the cases where there has been difficulty or delay in providing proof of age.

This will make no difference, I take it, to the present rule that it is the date of the application which counts, not the date upon which proof of age is produced. In other words, this will date back to the time at which the application is made, even though it may have been three or four months before age could be proved.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. I think many hon. members are not aware of the nature of the current provision. Suppose some one applies in July, after reaching age 70 in January and finds he cannot produce proof of age. Even though the provision of proof may take a year the pension will date back to the time at which the applicant actually qualified. Should an applicant have qualified before he applied-suppose he qualifies in January and applies in February-notwithstanding that it may be some months before he can produce proof of age, the pension would presently date back, not to the qualifying date but to the application date. This amendment will mean the pension does not date back to the date of application but can date back as far as a year before that date should the applicant be qualified.

I have one question to ask concerning these qualifications and the possibility that a qualified person may forget to make an application or choose not to do so for various reasons, some of which the hon. lady
Canada Pension Plan
has mentioned. Is there not some method, by using electronic machines, of finding out ahead of time the dates upon which a person will become eligible for a pension? Civil servants working on the scheme would then be able to advise prospective applicants ahead of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is possible, in the same way as we shall be starting this coming summer to warn parents of children who are reaching 16 about the youth allowances which continue through the ages of 17 and 18, provided the children go to school. However, we cannot rely completely on this because, as members will appreciate, people die and one cannot be sure that they will qualify for old age pension. Furthermore, we shall not necessarily have all the records in the first five year period. Records of birth, marriage and death are matters for provincial jurisdiction and though we have records covering the younger end of the scale-youth allowances and family allowances, for example-our records do not cover everyone who will reach the age of 65 in the earlier years. Thus there is no way by which we can automatically advise people who are approaching the time when they can draw a pension in these earlier years.
At the end of the five year period, of course, everyone in the country will know that they can get a pension at the age of 65. I might also point out that some people will be out of the country and that many will change their addresses; there is a high percentage of changes of address in this country. Many people will, no doubt, continue to apply for pensions through their members of parliament as at present.

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we are all aware of the significance and importance of clause 122. Indeed, as I stated earlier, I think it is a clause that the committee ought to defeat. I notice that those who might be persuaded to vote for it are here in good numbers. I hope that those who think the clause should be defeated get in here as well, before the vote on this clause is called. It will be no surprise to hon. members when I say that I spent a fair amount of time trying to figure out ways of presenting amendments to this bill that would achieve some of the changes that we in our party thought should be made. I made it clear on an earlier clause that I accept the rule that a private member cannot move an amendment that would directly involve the expenditure of moneys. In that case I drafted the amendment and offered it to the government. I am sorry that the government did not see fit to move it.
Another point concerning which I tried to find some way to draft an amendment was with respect to this proposal of the government that the paying of the pension at age 65 was to come about only by stages; in other words, that it would take five years to bring it into effect. When I looked at the draft of the earlier bill and when I thought of ways in which the government might prepare this amendment, I felt there was not any way in which a private member could move an amendment so that we could get a vote on the question, namely that the full pension should be paid at age 65, starting right now. I must extend my warmest thanks to the government, because the government itself has drafted the clauses in such a way that we do not need to move an amendment. All we need to do is be here in sufficient numbers to vote on this important clause.
If hon. members will take a look again at the bill they will see that in clause 119 as amended, which we have already passed, we

have declared that the old age security pension is to be paid to every person who has attained 65 years of age. There are certain other qualifications, but there is nothing in clause 119 that delays the implementation of that provision that the old age security pension be paid at age 65. However, the minister has pointed out that when one looks at clause 119 he has also to look at clause 122, because it does provide the qualification; but the qualification that is provided in clause 122 stands entirely on its own feet. The clause as a whole says that the provision already set out for the pension to be paid at age 65 is modified by this proposal that it be paid at age 69 in the year 1966, at age 68 in the year 1967, at 67 in the year 1968, at 66 in the year 1969, and that it shall be 1970 before it is paid at the age of 65. If we defeat clause 122 then the operative portion, so far as the eligible age is concerned, will be clause 119.
I hope, therefore, that those who feel the pension should come into effect right away will be here to vote against this clause.
I know that the Minister of National Revenue, and others for that matter, will no doubt, if this develops into a debate, again raise the question of cost. No one in this house is unaware of the fact that social benefits cost money. We are also aware of the fact that wealth is created socially, and we think it is proper that this wealth should get back to the people on a basis decided by parliament. But, Mr. Chairman, I feel I must again draw attention to something that has happened with respect to this question of taxation for the purposes of old age security. When the House of Commons, not last fall as the hon. member for Kindersley suggested, but the fall before last, in 1963, persuaded the government to raise the then old age security pension of $65 a month to $75 a month, the government said that it had to be matched by an increase in taxation. So the then 3 per cent tax on personal income for old age security was raised to 4 per cent. We were given the distinct understanding that this one percentage point increase was necessary to pay that $10. But, Mr. Chairman, when Bill No. C-136 was brought in, it had in it a proposal for an actuarially reduced old age security pension to be paid at ages below 70, working down to age 65. In fact, it included $51 a month in 1970 for those who would be 65 years of age. When we had this subject under discussion in the special joint committee we were told that the government had discovered it did not need to impose any additional taxation to pay $51 a month at

age 65, or $55.80 a month at age 66, $60.60 a month at age 67, and so on.
This was interesting to us, and we were given various explanations. My colleague from Timiskaming said this afternoon that we think the ceiling of $3,000 on the old age security tax should be removed. That has been our position ever since this tax was brought into being; but the experience we have had is that the increase in the old age security tax in 1963 originally was to provide only $10 to those over 70. Then it provided an actuarially reduced pension down to age 65; now it is producing a full pension down to age 65 by 1970. This suggests to us that if there was a little sharpening of the government pencil it would And that it could go the whole way and pay $75 at age 65 immediately.

They suggest that individuals aged 65 are entitled to old age security benefits, but only if they become age 65 in 1970. The original clause 121 of part IV of the bill evidenced this same type of illogical argument. Under the original provisions actuarially reduced old age security was envisaged. Under these provisions an individual could accept an old age security pension at age 65, but at an actuarially reduced amount of $51. Many hon. members during our committee proceedings pointed out in respect of this provision that it was illogical, because individuals reaching age 65 who were in need would accept the $51 per month and would be stuck with that amount for the rest of their lives. Apparently the government listened to those arguments at that time. Unfortunately the amendment now proposed by the government was not submitted to that committee. If it had been, perhaps the same complaints might have changed the government's mind again.
By what earthly reason should a person who reaches age 65 in 1970 be in greater need of old age security than a person who reaches 65 in 1966? By what remote argument of logic can the government justify such a proposition? How could anyone who understands the needs of elderly people justify a provision such as this?

Canada Pension Plan
I realize that when an instant benefit program is introduced, where everyone will receive certain benefits as of the day of inception, certain people will ask why the provisions were not adopted yesterday. However, when the government says in advance, and this is clearly spelled out in clause 122 of this bill as amended, that individuals who reach age 65 next year will not receive any benefits, but those who reach age 65 in 1970 will receive $75 a month, surely this is illogical and there will be a good reason for complaint. Furthermore, some of the individuals who will receive benefits at age 65 in 1970 will at the same time receive benefits from the Canada pension plan. It may be true that these benefits will not be great, but these people will be receiving something. On the other hand, individuals who attain the age of 65 in 1966 will not receive one penny from the Canada pension plan. I suggest that is one more inane feature of this proposal. I cannot understand the argument of the government in support of such a proposal as this.
If we provide an instant benefit as of this year some individuals will ask why these benefits were not provided earlier. In spite of that obvious fact this government is giving notice that it will provide old age security benefits to individuals who are 65 in 1970, but not to those who reach 65 before then. What more illogical argument could be presented by any government, particularly to a citizen of this country who at 65 in 1966 asks why he is not entitled to that which will be available to a citizen who reaches 65 in 1970? I am shocked by the government in its use of an argument such as this. I have never heard any more illogical explanation given in respect of any proposal.
