There is provision in section 91 of the Old Age Security Act for the governor in council to make certain regulations. One of them provides for the payment of benefits to a person or an agency on behalf of anyone who is incapacitated. Clause 123 was intended to be the corollary of those requirements. The requirements respecting the incapacity of a pensioner under the Old Age Security Act are subsections (1), (2) and (3) of regulation 13. In these instances, where the director has stated that a pensioner by reason of infirmity, illness, insanity or other cause is incapable of managing his own affairs he may direct that the pension be paid to an agency or an individual on his behalf. There is also a requirement that the agency or individual receiving the money has to account for it in a form which the director may indicate.
Normally, the authorization of an agency or body capable of acting for someone who is incapacitated in these circumstances is a matter of provincial law. Lawyers will be familiar with the term "public trustee". I think all the provinces have made arrangements in this respect though I am not certain which officers act in all cases. But this is a matter for the provincial governments-it is for them to say which individual, commercial or state agencies shall be accepted.
The situation may arise where a monthly pension cheque is the only asset of someone who has to become a patient at a mental hospital. It may be that a daughter or other relative has had to look after this aged person for some time, incurring doctors' and other bills. She may be able to show by affidavit or otherwise that these debts were incurred on the patient's behalf, and the cheque may then be sent to reimburse her. In each case it is a matter of who is qualified under the provincial law to act instead of and for the benefit of the person who is incapacitated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today on orders of the day I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) whether in view of the stand he had taken in respect of the civil rights question in the United States his government was prepared to
[The Chairman.]

introduce immediately legislation which would give the territorial franchise to those 10,000 people, mostly Eskimos, who live in those parts of the north where as yet, citizens, even though they pay territorial taxes, are deprived of the right to vote. At that point the Prime Minister replied that he could see no connection between a civil rights question in respect of Canada's northland and the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I did not raise this question today in an attempt to embarrass the Prime Minister or the government generally, but because, along with many other Canadians, I observed a demonstration on parliament hill yesterday and was impressed with the fact that people all over the world are concerned with an old, yet new concept-that everyone is really everyone else's neighbour, and that if one does not have the right to vote he is not free.
I raise this question also because I hope to capitalize on what I feel is a spirit sweeping the whole continent, and with the hope that in this way, by bringing the matter to the attention of hon. members in this chamber, 1 can impress upon them the necessity for changing the present situation. It is within the power of this House of Commons to see to it that not one more territorial election takes place in respect of which every adult individual 21 years of age and over, Eskimo or otherwise, is not entitled to vote.
Hon. members of this committee may realize that it was not until 1962 that the right to vote in federal elections was extended to the Keewatin district, the eastern Arctic and the central Arctic. Prior to that time there was no law preventing an Eskimo from voting, but he did not have any way of getting on the voters list. There was no machinery whereby individuals living in those areas of this country could get to a poll or have their names placed on a voting list.
Having regard to the territorial council, which is the embryonic equivalent of a provincial legislature, there are only four areas or constituencies of the territorial north. These four constituencies-not by accident-are those areas of the north populated predominantly by white people. That has been the pattern followed in the granting of franchises. Wherever there was a cluster of white people, who tended to be more vocal in fighting for their own interests, a territorial franchise was given-but nowhere else. Last November the council of the Northwest Territories unanimously passed a resolution requesting the federal parliament to see to it that the

territorial franchise was extended to all residents of the eastern Arctic, the Keewatin district and the central Arctic region, areas which are inhabited predominantly by Eskimo people.
I have been raising this matter ever since I came to the House of Commons. I brought it to the attention of this house when the Prime Minister made his statement in London last July 12 to the effect that the right to vote should not be granted along racial lines. He was attending the commonwealth conference at that time. My remarks at that time can be found at page 5380 of Hansard. I have raised this question on every opportunity I have had in this chamber. I have asked the government to extend the right to vote to all the people of the Northwest Territories.
At page 5971 of Hansard it will be found that I said the following in this regard:
Do not let 1964 end without being able to say to Canada, and in fact to Southern Rhodesia if we are going to give lectures, that every Canadian citizen over 21, regardless of where he may live in this country, has the right to vote for his own council.
The statement of the Prime Minister to the students yesterday, read by proxy, said, in part, this:
I honour those in Alabama or anywhere else who are lighting within the law for their rights as free citizens...
I know that the United States government is deeply concerned and is striving to remove the causes of this concern through its civil rights legislation.
I too, Mr. Speaker, know that the President of the United States is concerned. I want to know whether the Prime Minister of Canada is concerned. It is one thing to put a barricade before a courthouse in Selma, Alabama, to prevent people from registering. But it is another thing to provide no place at all for people to register, which is what we are doing in this country. I would ask whoever speaks for the government tonight, in a spirit of civil rights and in a spirit of co-operation and non-partisanship-and I am sure this request will draw universal support from the house-to amend the Northwest Territories Act by adding to it a provision to enable people who live anywhere in the north to vote. If we do not do this, if we cannot do it, or if we will not do it, then I say to the Prime Minister and to all members of this house, for God's sake let us at least quit sending telegrams of condolence to people who are prepared to give their time and their effort, if necessary their lives, to fight a civil

I am going to suggest to the hon. member for the Northwest Territories that I think there is a measure of anachronism in his complaint at this time. I think he is aware of the entire background. I also think he supported the party of which he is now a member in 1962, at which time he will surely recall that his party drew up two bills providing for the separation of the territories into the areas of Mackenzie and Nunassiaq. He will further recall that his party did nothing with these bills; they did not even bring them to the House of Commons.
If we go a little further we find the hon. member for Northwest Territories sitting in this house on July 8, 1963 when we introduced those bills which would, in part, have provided the reform for which he is pleading tonight. And what did he do? He opposed them day in and day out and fought the bills all the way through, not on this basis, I grant you; not on the basis that we were extending the franchise to the Eskimo people, but on other bases.
All I want to say is this: We want to be progressive. I think we have been progressive in respect to the territories, and we intend to be so in the future. I have been working very closely with the commissioner and the * council of the Northwest Territories. There seems to be in that body at the present time a degree of ferment which is healthy and progressive and good, and I am glad to see it.
I think we have a council, both in elected members and appointed members, which probably is more determined and vigorous than has been the case for some time. I know full well the resolutions they have passed, and which they have referred to us. I am not going to charge my hon. friend with anticipating what we are going to do, but I am going to tell him now that we are going to move very quickly in this field. It is a matter of policy which will be announced in the house in due course, and I think that when it is announced even he will be more than satisfied with our actions.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-PROVISION TO PERMIT ESKIMOS TO VOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday some of us had the opportunity of witnessing an inspiring demonstration here on parliament hill. Thousands of Canadian citizens gathered to express their belief in the fact that people are entitled to elementary justice. The question I asked today, Mr. Speaker, also deals with a case of what I believe to be injustice. One Jean Louis Henry, a man in his fifties, is in a maximum security cell in Kingston penitentiary facing imprisonment for the rest of his natural life. He was declared an habitual criminal by Magistrate Douglas Hume last December in Vancouver. His trial was held and sentence was passed while Henry was in another prison near Sudbury, 2,100 miles away.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that those of us who have been brought up to believe in the concept of British justice believe that a person is entitled, when he is accused of a crime, to know that he is accused. He is entitled to be present when he is accused. He is entitled to have counsel when his case is heard. He is entitled to enter a defence, and if he is found guilty he is entitled or his counsel is entitled to explain the circumstances in order that there may be some mercy. None of these conditions prevailed, so a man has been convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that the crown prosecutor was not appointed by the federal government and he is not directly responsible to the federal government. However, the crown prosecutor in Vancouver is taking action which has a very definite effect on the federal administration of justice. He is taking action under a section of the Criminal Code passed by the parliament of Canada. I want to say that I find it amazing that we have a crown prosecutor of this type in Canada in the year 1965. I think he would have been more suitable a couple of hundred years ago. At the time of the inquisition I can see him turning the screws or putting somebody on the rack. In the middle ages, I can see him chopping off somebody's hand because he stole a loaf of bread. I am told that in the last 30 years, in the whole of the province of Ontario less than 10 people have been declared habitual criminals. In the city of Vancouver in the last three years, 46 people have been declared habitual criminals and are now serving life sentences.


I think that the parliament of Canada, and the government at the time this section of the Criminal Code was enacted, never intended this section should be used as frequently as it is being used. I am told that there is a man 30 years old who has been declared an habitual criminal and who is now serving a life sentence. If he lives to the normal age at which people are living these days, he will serve 45 years in prison. Even if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) is not concerned about the morality of this situation, I suggest to him he look at the cost to the country. It is now costing us in the neighbourhood of $3,000 per year to keep a person in a federal penitentiary. This one man who is 30 years of age will cost the people of Canada some $135,000 before he dies. This is the kind of situation which is going on. One cannot blame the Minister of Justice for what the crown prosecutor in the city of Vancouver is doing, but the minister ought to take a hard look at what is happening.
If we have to have that provision in the Criminal Code-and I have some doubt that it serves any useful purpose-the minister ought to look at the clause which says that "the accused is entitled to be present at his hearing." Does that mean he has a right to be present at his hearing? The crown prosecutor in Vancouver takes the position that he may be present, but there is no responsibility on the crown to see he will be present. The Minister of Justice should quickly look at this section of the act to see whether it ought to be removed from the Criminal Code, amended or qualified.
If the kind of situation which has prevailed in Vancouver is going to continue, then very soon we will have to build another penitentiary to keep the people incarcerated whom this one crown prosecutor, with the approval of the attorney general of B.C., will have put in our prisons.
If we do not delete the whole section, then it seems to me the Minister of Justice ought to amend it to provide that this can only be done with the approval of the Minister of Justice. I would hope the minister will act in this matter very quickly because it seems to me that justice is being trampled in the dust if the crown prosecutor of Vancouver goes his mad way.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think any hon. member will find

very much to disagree with in the general principle cited by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). However, one additional fact that perhaps he should be made aware of is that in the particular case of Henry an appeal is now under way in the B.C. courts. Therefore I think we in this house should tread carefully in how we comment on that particular case, lest we give the appearance of prejudging the decision of the court. Certainly I on behalf of the government will be careful in anything I might say which could prejudge the court's decision in that case.
As the hon. member mentioned, the preventive detention provisions were added to the Criminal Code by the former government in the 1960-61 session, and it is rather ironic that a study by the home office in the United Kingdom has recommended that the British provisions, on which ours were modelled, should be deleted.
Section 662(l)(a) of the Criminal Code provides that "seven clear days notice" must be given the accused. Section 660(3) states that "the accused is entitled to be present at the hearing," and section 2(e) of the Canadian Bill of Rights provides that "no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to-
- (e) deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations.
These are the provisions of the law, but it falls on the B.C. courts to interpret them, and I would say that it is hoped these provisions of the law will be effective to protect the rights of the accused, and that the fundamental principles to which the hon. member made reference will be adequate to ensure justice to Mr. Henry in this case.
The government will be following the case with the greatest interest and, if the provisions of the law are inadequate, then the government will take action to remove the flaw. In the view of the government, which I think the hon. member would share, it is unthinkable that any man should be condemned in any proceedings, whether criminal proceedings or other proceedings, in absentia. It is unthinkable that he should be condemned in absentia when already incarcerated, as was this man in Burwash. The government will follow the case very closely and bring about any changes in the law indicated by the appeal court's decision.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) had chosen to answer a polite question from me this afternoon you would not be sitting in your chair at this late hour, nor would other hon. members be in theirs. He was asked a polite question, whether he would give any assurance that the policy of cattle grazing in the Riding Mountain national park would be continued, and whether the same policy would be continued in regard to the cutting of hay. It may not appear important to the minister, but it is very important to hundreds of farmers on each side of the Riding Mountain national park, on the south side in Marquette constituency and on the north side in the Dauphin constituency. There are hundreds of farmers who have depended on grazing their cattle in the park and on cutting hay in the park from the time the area was opened for settlement. These people are concerned, and for good reason. During the Christmas recess scores of delegations came to me because of rumours that no grazing permits and no hay cutting permits would be issued in 1965. They would not like to see a repetition of what happened in 1964 when the government chose to raise the hay cutting fee from 50 cents a ton to $5 a ton right in the middle of the hay cutting season. Those who came in early got permits at 50 cents a ton. Those who were a bit late had to pay $5, and they had no alternative because they needed the hay. I think the minister of northern affairs should order that some adjustment be made to make up for the discrepancy in price between those who bought their permits early and the others who bought them at a later date.
What distresses these farmers-and it distresses me too-is a letter I received from the minister dated March 3 in reply to my letter of January 12 or 13. I may say in passing that it took a long time to answer. The hon. gentleman gives reasons for his attitude and says, in part:
For these reasons grazing of livestock in a national park should be reduced to a minimum and grazing of cattle eventually eliminated.
This is very distressing to the people involved. One would think that the Riding Mountain national park was all parkland. But not one hundredth of it is developed as a park. The rest of it is a forest reserve. There is plenty of grass for all. During the

The price of cattle has gone up and people have been encouraged to increase their herds. They do not have sufficient pasture on their own land; they do not have enough hay.
